title: Exploring the robustness of permutation entropy analysis to differentiate between closed-eyes and open-eyes resting states
comment: This article may be downloaded for personal use only. Any other use requires prior permission of the author and AIP Publishing. This article appeared in Gancio, Juan, et al. "Exploring the robustness of permutation entropy analysis to differentiate between closed-eyes and open-eyes resting states." Chaos (2026), and may be found at https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0326211
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a noninvasive technology that is widely used to monitor brain states, and many efforts are focused on developing reliable and efficient data analysis methods for EEG recordings. Here, we apply ordinal analysis to the EEG recording of the resting state of 109 healthy subjects measured in two different conditions: with eyes closed (EC state) or eyes open (EO state). We study the robustness of the temporal permutation entropy ($PE$) and the spatial permutation entropy ($SPE$) with respect to the presence of blinking artifacts in the EO recordings, the duration of the recordings, and the number of EEG channels analyzed. We perform a paired statistical test to assess whether these quantities differ significantly in the EO and EC recordings of the same subject. We find that $PE$ and $SPE$ perform surprisingly well, as they detect significant differences when calculated from the raw signals, even within a short time interval ($PE$) or from a reduced number of electrodes ($SPE$).

AI.tldr: Ordinal analysis (temporal and spatial permutation entropy) robustly distinguishes eyes-closed from eyes-open resting EEG states in 109 healthy subjects, even with artifacts, short recordings, or few channels.
AI.motivation: EEG is a widely used noninvasive tool for monitoring brain states, creating a need for reliable and efficient data analysis methods for EEG recordings.
AI.method: Apply ordinal analysis to resting-state EEG of 109 healthy subjects in eyes-closed (EC) and eyes-open (EO) conditions. Test robustness of temporal permutation entropy (PE) and spatial permutation entropy (SPE) against blinking artifacts, recording duration, and number of EEG channels. Use paired statistical tests to compare EO vs. EC within subjects.
AI.result: PE and SPE perform surprisingly well, detecting significant EO/EC differences from raw signals, even within a short time interval (PE) or from a reduced number of electrodes (SPE).
AI.conclusion: Ordinal-analysis measures (PE and SPE) are robust and efficient indicators of brain state, suitable even for short and/or low-channel EEG recordings.

title: 2D reaction-diffusion model-based biopsy simulation for dynamic tumor growth parameter estimation
summary: Once diagnosed, cancer requires a fast, reliable and preferably cost-efficient assessment of the current state and potential progression of the disease. A new method for estimating tumor cell diffusivity $D$ and proliferation rate $γ$ in the context of the mechanistic reaction-diffusion equation from single-point-in-time routine biopsies aims to deliver just that, and quantities computed from the parameter estimates have recently been tested as a new biomarkers for risk-stratification in radiotherapy. Here, we extend the findings of this previous work by providing a first theoretical validation. The method is applied to in-silico biopsies which are generated by solving the two-dimensional reaction-diffusion equation for different growth terms (exponential and logistic) with a Dirac-Delta initial condition, and transforming the continuous results into spatial point patterns via a form of reverse coarse-graining. If no information about tumor age is used, in short-term experiments the original dispersion length $\sqrt{D/γ}$ could be retrieved with a relative root mean squared error (RRMSE) of around 8% and an $\text{R}^2$-value of 0.97. In long-term experiments, the RRMSEs ranged from 8 to 14% and the $\text{R}^2$-values from 0.75 to 0.98. The scaled front velocity $\sqrt{D \cdotγ}$, which can only be estimated if information about tumor age is available, was retrieved with an RRMSE of 7% and an $\text{R}^2$ of 0.98 in both, the short-term and the long-term experiments.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a first theoretical validation of a method for estimating tumor cell diffusivity D and proliferation rate γ from single-point-in-time biopsies via a reaction-diffusion model, tested on in-silico biopsies.
AI.motivation: Cancer diagnosis requires fast, reliable, and cost-efficient assessment of disease state and progression. A prior method estimating tumor cell diffusivity and proliferation rate from routine single-timepoint biopsies has shown promise as a biomarker for radiotherapy risk-stratification, but lacked theoretical validation.
AI.method: The estimation method is applied to in-silico biopsies generated by solving the 2D reaction-diffusion equation with Dirac-Delta initial conditions and different growth terms (exponential and logistic), converting continuous results into spatial point patterns via reverse coarse-graining.
AI.result: Without tumor age information, the dispersion length √(D/γ) was recovered with ~8% RRMSE and R²=0.97 in short-term experiments; in long-term experiments RRMSE ranged 8–14% and R² 0.75–0.98. The scaled front velocity √(D·γ), requiring tumor age, was recovered with 7% RRMSE and R²=0.98 in both short- and long-term experiments.
AI.conclusion: The method yields accurate parameter estimates for tumor cell diffusivity and proliferation rate, supporting its potential as a biomarker, though accuracy is somewhat lower in long-term experiments.

title: Foundation-model-based multi-label phenotyping of combined hyperkinetic movement disorders
comment: 29 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables, 1 supplementary table. Submitted to Artificial Intelligence in Medicine. Code: https://github.com/xaviervasques/cody-sam3 ; data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22232609
summary: Movement disorders (MDs) frequently co-occur, yet phenomenological and severity assessment shows substantial inter-rater variability. Markerless video could improve reproducibility, but prior work is largely single-symptom, depends on standardized acquisition, and lacks validation and transfer across ages and sites. We combined two foundation models into one frozen backbone: Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) for dense, per-frame markerless segmentation summarized into geometric, contour and grid kinematic signals, and TabICLv2, a tabular foundation model, for in-context multi-label classification of eight hyperkinetic MD phenomenologies. Trained on standardized recordings of 21 adults and 4 controls, it transferred unchanged to two independent datasets, pediatric (n=12) and tremor-dominant adult (n=20), assessed with the CODY-SAMP scale; only the patient-level decision step was recalibrated per site. Under clinician consensus labels, false positives fell to zero in both datasets. Dystonia recovered perfectly (7/7 pediatric; 15/15 adult held-out), chorea fully in children (3/3), and tremor was recovered in adults (11/15) once a tremor-rich cohort made it evaluable, through recalibration alone. Per-region effect-size analysis gave clinically coherent, phenomenology-specific signals and identified myoclonus as the principal failure. Against YOLOv8 sparse keypoints, the dense representation matched under clinician permissive labels (Jaccard 0.63 vs 0.63) and was markedly more robust under clinician-label consensus (0.93 vs 0.76). This frozen foundation-model backbone with light per-site calibration yields transferable, interpretable, conservative multi-label phenotyping of co-occurring hyperkinetic MDs across ages and from standardized to routine video, adding robustness on high-confidence, clinician-agreed labels. Prospective multi-centre validation is required before clinical use.

AI.tldr: A frozen two-foundation-model backbone (SAM 3 for markerless video segmentation + TabICLv2 for multi-label classification) phenotypes eight co-occurring hyperkinetic movement disorders, transferring across pediatric and adult datasets with only per-site recalibration, achieving zero false positives under clinician consensus.
AI.motivation: Movement disorders frequently co-occur, but phenomenological and severity assessment suffers from substantial inter-rater variability. Markerless video could improve reproducibility, yet prior work is largely single-symptom, requires standardized acquisition, and lacks validation and transfer across ages and sites.
AI.method: Combined two foundation models into one frozen backbone: SAM 3 for dense per-frame markerless segmentation summarized into geometric, contour, and grid kinematic signals, and TabICLv2 (tabular foundation model) for in-context multi-label classification of eight hyperkinetic MD phenomenologies. Against YOLOv8 sparse keypoints, dense representation matched under permissive labels (Jaccard 0.63 vs 0.63) and was more robust under consensus (0.93 vs 0.76).

title: From daylight to darkness: a nonlocal model of circadian activity cycles
summary: An animal's ability to perceive its surroundings, as well as the ecological interactions it experiences, can be strongly influenced by the sleep patterns of both itself and surrounding species. Animals with limited sensory capabilities may struggle to navigate their habitat at night, while in a predator-prey system, it may be detrimental for prey to be inactive while predators are awake and hunting. Here, we develop a general mathematical framework to study these interactions using partial differential equations, incorporating activity cycles and daylight-dependent perception into existing models of animal movement. We show that both the dominant sensory mode and the length of daylight are key factors determining the strength of aggregation in social species. Extending this framework to a two-species predator-prey system, we use game-theoretic approaches to show that the equilibrium sleep strategy of each species is shaped not only by its own sensory capabilities, but also by those of its ecological opponent. Depending on the sensory capabilities of the two species, equilibrium strategies may consist of a single sleep pattern or a combination of multiple sleep patterns.

AI.tldr: A PDE-based framework incorporating activity cycles and daylight-dependent perception shows how sensory mode and daylight length drive aggregation in social species, and that equilibrium sleep strategies in predator-prey systems depend on both species' sensory capabilities.
AI.motivation: Sleep patterns of an animal and surrounding species strongly influence perception and ecological interactions. Limited sensory capabilities can hinder nighttime navigation, and in predator-prey systems, inactivity during predator activity can be detrimental. This motivates a general mathematical framework to study such sleep-perception-ecology interactions.
AI.method: The authors develop a general mathematical framework using partial differential equations, incorporating activity cycles and daylight-dependent perception into existing animal movement models. They extend it to a two-species predator-prey system and apply game-theoretic approaches to determine equilibrium sleep strategies.
AI.result: Both the dominant sensory mode and the length of daylight are key factors determining aggregation strength in social species. In the predator-prey system, each species' equilibrium sleep strategy is shaped not only by its own sensory capabilities but also by those of its ecological opponent. Equilibrium strategies may consist of a single sleep pattern or a combination of multiple sleep patterns, depending on the sensory capabilities of the two species.
AI.conclusion: Sleep/perception interactions can be captured with a PDE framework where sensory mode, daylight, and cross-species sensory capabilities jointly determine aggregation and equilibrium sleep strategies, which may be single or mixed patterns.

title: Chaotic Dynamics-Regulated Topological Learning for Patient-Specific Preictal State Identification
comment: 23 pages, 5 figures. Code available at https://github.com/Wzhgeek/CDRTL
summary: Epileptic seizures arise from complex, nonlinear interactions within brain networks, yet reliable electroencephalographic (EEG) prediction remains challenging due to the nonstationary and heterogeneous nature of neural dynamics. Existing methods typically analyze EEG data as static or weakly time-dependent snapshots, overlooking the intrinsic dynamics and lacking the geometric sensitivity to capture the hierarchical, localized evolution of the epileptogenic zone. To address these limitations, we propose an offline, patient-specific evaluation of chaotic dynamics-regulated topological learning (CDRTL) for distinguishing preictal from interictal EEG states. This framework unifies chaotic dynamics, multiscale algebraic topology, and local network differentiation. Specifically, we partition EEG signals into discrete functional subnets based on correlation strengths, capturing the multi-scale connectivity of the brain. By modeling each node as a Lorenz oscillator, we embed the underlying chaotic dynamics into the network architecture. We then apply the persistent Laplacian to simultaneously extract topological invariants and geometric shape evolution through harmonic and non-harmonic spectral analysis. Additionally, a node-removal topological differentiation strategy isolates localized neural contributions. Our framework was evaluated on the CHB-MIT database using balanced preictal and interictal labels and stratified channel-level cross-validation within each patient. The results support offline discrimination of preictal and interictal channel-level nodes within fixed patient-specific networks. Because representations are constructed from the complete network, including held-out unlabeled nodes, before cross-validation, the reported performance is specific to this transductive setting and does not establish generalization to unseen EEG windows, seizures, or patients.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CDRTL, an offline patient-specific framework combining chaotic dynamics, multiscale algebraic topology, and local network differentiation to distinguish preictal from interictal EEG states, evaluated on CHB-MIT in a transductive setting.
AI.motivation: Reliable EEG seizure prediction is hard due to nonstationary, heterogeneous neural dynamics. Existing methods treat EEG as static or weakly time-dependent snapshots, missing intrinsic dynamics and geometric sensitivity needed to capture hierarchical, localized evolution of the epileptogenic zone.
AI.method: CDRTL unifies chaotic dynamics, multiscale algebraic topology, and local network differentiation. EEG signals are partitioned into functional subnets by correlation strength; each node is modeled as a Lorenz oscillator to embed chaotic dynamics. Persistent Laplacian extracts topological invariants and geometric shape evolution via harmonic/non-harmonic spectral analysis, plus a node-removal strategy isolates localized neural contributions.
AI.result: Evaluated on CHB-MIT with balanced preictal/interictal labels and stratified channel-level cross-validation per patient. Results support offline discrimination of preictal vs. interictal channel-level nodes within fixed patient-specific networks. Performance is specific to the transductive setting and does not establish generalization to unseen EEG windows, seizures, or patients.
AI.conclusion: CDRTL offers an offline, patient-specific means of distinguishing preictal from interictal EEG states, but claims are limited to a transductive setting; generalization to unseen data or patients remains unestablished.

title: Minimality in Reflexive and Stoichiometric Autocatalysis
comment: 37 Pages: 31 main text and 6 SI. 10 Figures: 4 in main text and 6 in SI
summary: Autocatalysis, the ability of a chemical subsystem to sustain its own constituents when supplied with sufficient food molecules, has been closely related to the origin of life on Earth. Emerging from Wilhelm Ostwald's considerations about an explicit autocatalytic reaction, different notions of autocatalysis have been developed over the years. The two most prominent are reflexively autocatalytic F-generated sets (RAFs) and stoichiometric autocatalysis. After having shown that each RAFs is, under reasonable conditions, in general stoichiometrically autocatalytic, we examine here the relationship between the two notions of minimality: irreducible RAFs and autocatalytic cores. To this end, we overcome the obstacle that RAFs and stoichiometric autocatalysis have been formalized in distinct systems of chemical reactions, i.e., catalytic reaction systems (CRS) and chemical reaction networks (CRNs), respectively. We show that reactions in a CRS constitute equivalence classes of reactions of the corresponding CRNs w.r.t. their specific catalyzations. Using the fact that CRN and CRS can be canonically identified whenever each CRS reaction is associated with a single catalyzation, we demonstrate that the Kőnig graph of a monocatalyzed, irreducible RAF is composed of strong blocks devoid of food and waste species that are separated by reaction vertices, each of which contains an autocatalytic core. In fact, a single irreducible RAF can, in general, contain exponentially many autocatalytic cores.

AI.tldr: This paper clarifies the relationship between two notions of autocatalysis—reflexively autocatalytic F-generated sets (RAFs) and stoichiometric autocatalysis—and their minimal forms (irreducible RAFs vs. autocatalytic cores), showing that a single irreducible RAF can contain exponentially many autocatalytic cores.
AI.motivation: Autocatalysis is central to origin-of-life theories, but two prominent formalizations (RAFs and stoichiometric autocatalysis) developed from Ostwald's ideas exist in distinct frameworks, leaving the relationship between their minimality notions unclear.
AI.method: The authors bridge catalytic reaction systems (CRS) and chemical reaction networks (CRNs) by showing CRS reactions form equivalence classes of CRN reactions under specific catalyzations. Using canonical identification when each CRS reaction has a single catalyzation, they analyze the Kőnig graph of monocatalyzed irreducible RAFs.
AI.result: Every RAF is, under reasonable conditions, generally stoichiometrically autocatalytic. For a monocatalyzed irreducible RAF, its Kőnig graph consists of strong blocks free of food/waste species separated by reaction vertices, each containing an autocatalytic core. A single irreducible RAF can contain exponentially many autocatalytic cores.
AI.conclusion: The two notions of autocatalysis are shown to be related: RAFs are generally stoichiometrically autocatalytic, yet the minimal structures differ substantially, with irreducible RAFs potentially harboring exponentially many autocatalytic cores.

title: Demographic inference of pathogen-infected populations from partially observed transmission forests
summary:
Genomic epidemiology has several methods for identifying which sampled individuals are linked by close proximity in the transmission chain, whether by grouping them into clusters under a genetic distance threshold or by identifying probable direct transmission pairs. Individuals found to have no sampled neighbours---singletons---are usually set aside. We argue that they are informative. Whether any two sampled individuals prove to be linked depends on the size of the sampling frame and the number of independent lineage introductions into it, and thus the balance of linked and unlinked individuals is itself data about these quantities.
  We formalise this by treating the intersection of a transmission tree with a sampling frame as a labelled rooted forest, from which a fixed number of nodes are sampled uniformly at random. Using the all-minors matrix-tree theorem, we derive a closed-form expression for the number of labelled rooted $k$-forests on $N$ nodes in which a specified set of nodes is independent. From this we obtain, again in closed form, the probability that a sample of a given size contains no linked individuals at all, and the likelihood of an arbitrary observed configuration of clusters, both when the transmission structure within each is known, and when only the cluster sizes are.
  The approach is closer to a survey, or to mark-recapture, than to conventional phylodynamic model fitting: the information comes from the linkage structure of a single sample alone with no assumptions regarding pathogen dynamics. We outline three applications: power calculations for prospective studies, a test of the uniform sampling assumption that underlies the reading of clusters as transmission hotspots, and demographic inference itself. We finally set out the assumptions that a more flexible implementation would need to relax.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that genomic-epidemiology "singletons" (sampled individuals with no linked neighbours) carry information, and develops a survey/mark-recapture-style formalism—based on labelled rooted forests and the all-minors matrix-tree theorem—to derive closed-form probabilities for sample linkage configurations and use them for study design, sampling tests, and demographic inference.
AI.motivation: Standard genomic epidemiology focuses on clusters and probable transmission pairs, discarding singletons as uninformative. The authors argue this is a mistake: whether sampled individuals appear linked depends on the sampling-frame size and the number of independent lineage introductions, so the balance of linked versus unlinked individuals is itself data about those quantities.
AI.method: They treat the intersection of a transmission tree with a sampling frame as a labelled rooted forest, from which a fixed number of nodes is sampled uniformly at random. Using the all-minors matrix-tree theorem, they derive a closed-form count of labelled rooted k-forests on N nodes in which a specified node set is independent, yielding closed-form probabilities that a sample contains no linked individuals and likelihoods for observed cluster configurations—both when within-cluster transmission structure is known and when only cluster sizes are.
AI.result: Closed-form expressions for the number of labelled rooted k-forests with an independent specified node set, the probability of a sample containing no linked individuals, and the likelihood of arbitrary observed cluster configurations (structure-known and size-only cases).
AI.conclusion: The approach resembles a survey or mark-recapture design rather than conventional phylodynamic model fitting, using only the linkage structure of a single sample without assumptions about pathogen dynamics. Three applications are outlined: power calculations for prospective studies, a test of the uniform-sampling assumption underlying cluster-based hotspot interpretation, and demographic inference. The authors also set out assumptions a more flexible implementation would need to relax.

title: From Biological Precursors to Artificial Cognition: Consciousness, Embodiment, and the MEM Architecture
summary: This article asks under what conditions artificial intelligence could warrant a rational attribution of consciousness. Linguistic ability, multimodality, memory, planning, action control, and humanoid embodiment are not sufficient evidence of phenomenal experience. Biological precursors such as excitability, homeostasis, neural networks, and hierarchical representation instead identify functions whose counterparts may be engineered. The paper compares conventional LLMs, hybrid h-LLMs, vision-language-action systems, and embodied agents with the Motivated Emotional Mind (MEM) architecture. MEM adds receptor-grounded representations, regulatory self-monitoring and interoception, affect, semblion-based associative memory, and re-entry into lower sensory and interoceptive maps. A related formulation defines a phenomenal state as a dynamic, integrated state of the whole embodied system in which sensor-grounded modal content is recurrently stabilized and coupled to a suprathreshold interoceptive representation of the system's regulatory state. The mathematical model of MEM published on arXiv specifies implementable relations among these components and makes the proposal more precise and testable. Comparative and causal tests in humans, invertebrates, and artificial systems could strengthen or weaken the MEM capabilities. MEM is therefore presented as a falsifiable research program requiring empirical validation and ethical caution.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that consciousness attributions to AI require specific architectural features—not just language, multimodality, or embodiment. It proposes the Motivated Emotional Mind (MEM) as a falsifiable research program, defining phenomenal states via recurrently stabilized sensor-grounded content coupled to interoceptive representations of the system's regulatory state.
AI.motivation: To clarify under what conditions artificial intelligence could rationally be attributed consciousness, since common markers (linguistic ability, multimodality, memory, planning, action control, humanoid embodiment) are insufficient evidence of phenomenal experience.
AI.method: Compares conventional LLMs, hybrid h-LLMs, vision-language-action systems, and embodied agents against the MEM architecture, which integrates receptor-grounded representations, regulatory self-monitoring and interoception, affect, semblion-based associative memory, and re-entry into lower sensory and interoceptive maps. A mathematical model of MEM specifies implementable relations among components, and a related formulation defines phenomenal states as dynamic, integrated whole-system states where sensor-grounded modal content is recurrently stabilized and coupled to a suprathreshold interoceptive representation of the regulatory state.
AI.result: Biological precursors (excitability, homeostasis, neural networks, hierarchical representation) identify engineerable functions, whereas current AI markers do not suffice for consciousness. The MEM model makes the proposal precise, implementable, and testable via comparative and causal tests in humans, invertebrates, and artificial systems.
AI.conclusion: MEM is offered as a falsifiable research program that could be strengthened or weakened by empirical tests, requiring validation and ethical caution before any consciousness attribution to AI.

title: Binding-Motivated Contextuality: A Cross-Domain Cyclic Test in Perception and Judgment
summary: Perceptual binding and the contextuality of judgment are studied apart, in psychophysics and decision research. We argue they share one obstruction: a nonzero class in $H^1$ of a presheaf with no global section -- though only contextuality is tested, since binding's obstruction vanishes. We build on sheaf formulations of predictive coding (Seely 2025) and contextuality (Abramsky & Brandenburger 2011): a cyclic set of pairwise judgments admits a global (noncontextual) explanation exactly when the cyclic (Suppes-Zanotti / n-cycle) inequalities hold. Its obstruction is measured by the complete contextual fraction CF (Abramsky, Barbosa & Mansfield 2017), not the weaker Cech invariant, which certifies contextuality but can miss it (Caru 2017). Penrose (1992) classifies the continuous tribar by $H^1$ over the multiplicative group $\mathbb{R}^+$ of depths -- but the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ case is what we test. We build the perceptual arena from two binary judgments per cyclic-dominance pairing, realizing the same frustrated-cycle obstruction as the survey. The central test is cross-domain: one cohort performs both; shared mechanism predicts a correlation between the arenas' signed obstruction margins -- CF before clamping -- which neither field has measured. Both are inconsistency scores, so a bare correlation is confounded by general response consistency. The prediction is therefore confound-residualized: the correlation must survive partialling out a general-consistency factor from a variance- and reliability-matched control. A sufficiently precise null would count against that account, provided the preregistered reliability checks pass and the control does not load on the obstruction. All three tests are designed but unrun.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that perceptual binding and judgment contextuality share the same cohomological obstruction (a nonzero H^1 class with no global section), though only contextuality is empirically testable since binding's obstruction vanishes. It designs three unrun tests: measuring contextuality via the complete contextual fraction, requiring a reliability-checked control, and testing a confound-residualized cross-domain correlation.
AI.motivation: Perceptual binding (psychophysics) and contextuality (decision research) are studied separately, but the authors argue both are obstructed by the same nonzero cohomology class. Because binding's obstruction vanishes, only contextuality can be empirically tested, motivating a unified sheaf-theoretic framework.
AI.method: Builds on sheaf formulations of predictive coding and contextuality. Uses cyclic Suppes-Zanotti / n-cycle inequalities to characterize global (noncontextual) explanations, measures the obstruction via the complete contextual fraction (not the weaker Cech invariant), and constructs a perceptual arena with two binary judgments per cyclic-dominance pairing. Central test: a cross-domain correlation between signed obstruction margins (CF before clamping), confound-residualized against a general-consistency factor from a variance- and reliability-matched control.
AI.result: No results yet -- all three tests are designed but unrun (preregistered reliability checks and control constraints specified).
AI.conclusion: The shared-mechanism account predicts a cross-domain correlation surviving confound residualization; a sufficiently precise null (with passing reliability checks and a control not loading on the obstruction) would count against it. The empirical work remains to be executed.

title: Retracing the Process of Translation: Proteome-wide mapping of stable transcriptomic predictors of protein abundance in cancer cell lines
comment: Accepted for oral presentation at ISCB-AI 2026
summary:
Understanding the relationship between gene expression and protein abundance is central to molecular and systems biology. While gene expression reflects transcriptional activity, proteins are the functional molecules that determine cellular phenotypes. However, numerous post-transcriptional and translational regulatory layers complicate this relationship, and prior studies have reported only weak to moderate correlations between RNA and protein levels. Predicting protein abundance from transcriptomic data remains challenging, but it is a valuable goal for biological insight, especially when proteomic data is limited or unavailable.
  In this study, we applied a large-scale, Ridge regression-based feature selection strategy to identify predictive gene expression features for each of 8,423 proteins across 940 cancer cell lines. To our knowledge, this is the first work to perform such comprehensive protein-wise feature selection at this scale. Our analysis revealed both globally predictive and context-specific gene features. These included biologically meaningful modules such as immune-related genes, HOX transcription factor targets, and cytoskeletal components. The models identified stable candidate gene-protein associations that remained interpretable at the level of individual proteins and recurrent transcriptomic predictor patterns.
  Our approach enables interpretable modeling of protein expression from transcriptomic data and provides insight into transcriptomic features associated with protein abundance. This framework may support hypothesis generation, protein imputation in incomplete datasets, and deeper understanding of post-transcriptional regulation in cancer biology.

AI.tldr: The paper applies Ridge regression-based feature selection to predict 8,423 proteins from transcriptomic data across 940 cancer cell lines, identifying interpretable gene-protein associations including immune, HOX, and cytoskeletal modules.
AI.motivation: Gene expression reflects transcriptional activity but proteins determine phenotypes; post-transcriptional and translational regulation weaken RNA-protein correlations. Predicting protein abundance from transcriptomic data is valuable, especially when proteomic data is limited, yet remains challenging.
AI.method: A large-scale, Ridge regression-based feature-selection strategy was applied to identify predictive gene expression features for each of 8,423 proteins across 940 cancer cell lines—claimed as the first comprehensive protein-wise feature selection at this scale.
AI.result: The analysis revealed both globally predictive and context-specific features, including biologically meaningful modules (immune-related genes, HOX transcription factor targets, cytoskeletal components), and stable, interpretable candidate gene-protein associations with recurrent transcriptomic predictor patterns.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables interpretable modeling of protein expression from transcriptomic data, supporting hypothesis generation, protein imputation in incomplete datasets, and deeper understanding of post-transcriptional regulation in cancer biology.

title: Decoding enzyme-substrate interaction topology reveals principles underlying catalytic efficiency and mutational outcomes
summary: The enzyme turnover number (kcat) defines catalytic efficiency and constrains quantitative models of metabolism, yet the molecular determinants governing kcat and its response to mutation remain poorly understood. Measurements are sparse and labor-intensive, and most computational approaches provide numerical predictions without explaining how enzyme-substrate interactions shape catalytic outcomes. A central challenge is therefore to identify the topological principles that determine where mutations act and how their functional outcomes are encoded within the enzyme-substrate interaction network. Here, we show that catalytic efficiency and mutational effects can be interpreted through enzyme-substrate interaction topology. We developed Interkcat, an interpretable bidirectional cross-attention framework that captures reciprocal coordination between protein residues and substrate atoms. Optimized on a unified benchmark, Interkcat achieves state-of-the-art predictive performance (R2 = 0.701). From its learned representations, we derive an Interaction Topology Score (ITS) that identifies sequence regions statistically enriched for mutation-sensitive sites without explicit structural inputs. We further demonstrate that higher-order topological features distinguish opposing mutational outcomes: lethal mutations disrupt coordinated networks, whereas activity-preserving or enhancing mutations retain sparse, globally organized coupling. These findings establish interaction topology as a unifying principle linking enzyme sequence, catalytic efficiency, and evolutionary perturbation.

AI.tldr: Interkcat, an interpretable bidirectional cross-attention framework, predicts kcat (R2=0.701) and reveals that enzyme-substrate interaction topology determines mutation-sensitive sites and mutational outcomes.
AI.motivation: kcat governs catalytic efficiency and metabolic models, but its molecular determinants and mutational responses are poorly understood. Measurements are sparse and most computational methods give numerical predictions without explaining how enzyme-substrate interactions shape catalysis. Identifying topological principles of where mutations act and how outcomes are encoded is a key challenge.
AI.method: Developed Interkcat, an interpretable bidirectional cross-attention framework capturing reciprocal coordination between protein residues and substrate atoms, optimized on a unified benchmark. Derived an Interaction Topology Score (ITS) from learned representations to identify mutation-sensitive sequence regions without structural inputs.
AI.result: Interkcat achieves state-of-the-art kcat prediction (R2=0.701). ITS identifies sequence regions enriched for mutation-sensitive sites without explicit structures. Higher-order topological features distinguish opposing mutational outcomes: lethal mutations disrupt coordinated networks, while activity-preserving/enhancing mutations retain sparse, globally organized coupling.
AI.conclusion: Interaction topology is a unifying principle linking enzyme sequence, catalytic efficiency, and evolutionary perturbation.

title: Adapting Boltz-2 with limited experimental activity data improves early enrichment in virtual screening
summary: Virtual screening aims to prioritize active compounds from large chemical libraries within a limited experimental budget. When applying Boltz-2 to virtual screening, a key challenge is how to use limited experimental data from the target assay to improve the prioritization of active compounds. We investigated whether fine-tuning the Boltz-2 affinity heads with a small number of binary activity labels could improve early enrichment of active compounds in hit discovery. We compared fine-tuning with 40-300 labels in a retrospective evaluation on eight MF-PCBA targets. With 300 activity measurements, fine-tuning increased the number of actives in the top 1% by a geometric mean of 1.77-fold across the eight targets and improved average precision (AP) by 2.14-fold relative to the control without fine-tuning. We also investigated whether rescoring a subset of candidates could retain the improvement in hit recovery by reranking only the top-ranked Boltz-2 candidates with the fine-tuned head. Restricting rescoring to approximately 10% of the evaluation set retained hit recovery comparable to full rescoring. These findings show that affinity-head fine-tuning with limited activity labels improves early enrichment with Boltz-2 and that this benefit can be retained when rescoring a restricted set of candidates.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning Boltz-2 affinity heads with 40-300 binary activity labels improves early enrichment in virtual screening, boosting top 1% actives by 1.77-fold and AP by 2.14-fold across eight MF-PCBA targets; restricting rescoring to ~10% of candidates retains most of the gain.
AI.motivation: Virtual screening must prioritize active compounds under limited experimental budgets. When using Boltz-2, it is unclear how to leverage scarce target-assay data to better rank actives, motivating investigation of whether fine-tuning the affinity heads with few binary labels can improve hit discovery.
AI.method: The authors fine-tuned Boltz-2 affinity heads using 40-300 binary activity labels and evaluated retrospectively on eight MF-PCBA targets against a no-fine-tuning control. They also tested whether reranking only the top-ranked Boltz-2 candidates (rescoring ~10% of the evaluation set) could retain the improvement versus full rescoring.
AI.result: With 300 activity measurements, fine-tuning increased actives in the top 1% by a geometric mean of 1.77-fold and improved average precision by 2.14-fold across the eight targets. Rescoring ~10% of candidates retained hit recovery comparable to full rescoring.
AI.conclusion: Affinity-head fine-tuning with limited activity labels improves Boltz-2's early enrichment in virtual screening, and this benefit persists when rescoring only a restricted subset of candidates, supporting cost-efficient hit discovery.

title: Phylogenetic Inference and the Stickiness of Fréchet Means, via Precise Asymptotics of an Embedded Random Walk
summary: A well-known phenomenon in statistical analyses of populations of phylogenetic trees in the Billera-Holmes-Vogtmann space is that the topology of the Fréchet mean tree can contain multifurcations (i.e., internal nodes with more than two children), which raises the practical question of whether this reflects a population-level branching structure (hard polytomy) or merely sampling variability in the data (soft polytomy). This is an instance of the more general phenomenon of "stickiness" in non-Euclidean statistics, whereby the sample Fréchet mean in certain non-positively curved stratified spaces becomes permanently trapped in a lower-dimensional stratum. In this work, we identify a particular multidimensional random walk embedded within the Fréchet mean process, and we show that the time at which stickiness occurs is determined by the largest last-passage time above zero of the coordinates of this random walk. Using this representation, we develop a fully nonparametric procedure for estimating the probability that trifurcations in a sample Fréchet mean tree will bifurcate at some future time if more observations are collected. Lastly, we apply our methodology to a problem in phylogenetics where we consider whether an observed trifurcation in the species tree of primates, glires, and tree shrews is genuinely trifurcated at the population level.

AI.tldr: The paper characterizes "stickiness" of Fréchet means in BHV tree space using a multidimensional random walk, and provides a nonparametric method to estimate the probability that a trifurcation will eventually resolve into a bifurcation as more data are collected.
AI.motivation: Multifurcations in Fréchet mean trees in Billera-Holmes-Vogtmann space raise the question of whether they reflect a true population-level branching structure (hard polytomy) or just sampling variability (soft polytomy). This is an instance of "stickiness" in non-Euclidean statistics, where the sample Fréchet mean gets trapped in a lower-dimensional stratum.
AI.method: The authors identify a multidimensional random walk embedded in the Fréchet mean process. They show that the time at which stickiness occurs is determined by the largest last-passage time above zero of the coordinates of this random walk. Using this representation, they develop a fully nonparametric procedure for estimating the probability that trifurcations in a sample Fréchet mean tree will bifurcate at some future time with more observations.
AI.result: They derive a representation linking stickiness time to the largest last-passage time above zero of the embedded random walk's coordinates, enabling estimation of the probability that an observed trifurcation will resolve (bifurcate) as more data are collected.
AI.conclusion: They apply the methodology to phylogenetics, examining whether an observed trifurcation in the species tree of primates, glires, and tree shrews is genuinely trifurcated at the population level.

title: Learning Dynamic Neural Evidence Representations for Time-Adaptive Brain-Computer Interfaces
summary: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) decode neural activity into commands, yet most existing systems rely on fixed-window decoding that may result in redundant observation or unreliable predictions due to insufficient evidence. Adaptive temporal decision-making (ATDM) addresses this accuracy-time trade-off by progressively accumulating EEG evidence and deciding when to stop. However, existing EEG encoders are mainly designed for fixed-window decoding and may not provide reliable state representations under variable observation lengths. In addition, current ATDM-oriented encoders are typically tailored to specific EEG paradigms, limiting their applicability across different BCI tasks. To address these limitations, we propose ProtoTrigger, a two-stage prototype learning-based EEG state encoder for ATDM. ProtoTrigger uses prototype matching to extract stable local EEG embeddings and prototype-based attention to aggregate decision-relevant temporal evidence during progressive observation. Offline evaluations across three EEG paradigms demonstrated state-of-the-art accuracy-time trade-offs and strong generalizability across different EEG paradigms. An online human-in-the-loop augmented reality-based BCI experiment further demonstrated its real-time feasibility. These results suggest that ProtoTrigger provides a general EEG state encoding framework for efficient ATDM-based BCI systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ProtoTrigger, a two-stage prototype-learning EEG state encoder for adaptive temporal decision-making (ATDM), achieving state-of-the-art accuracy-time trade-offs across three EEG paradigms plus online feasibility in an AR-based BCI experiment.
AI.motivation: Fixed-window BCI decoding can cause redundant observation or unreliable predictions due to insufficient evidence; though ATDM addresses this accuracy-time trade-off, existing EEG encoders are designed for fixed-window decoding, struggle with variable observation lengths, and are typically tailored to specific paradigms, limiting cross-task applicability.
AI.method: ProtoTrigger, a two-stage prototype learning-based EEG state encoder for ATDM: prototype matching extracts stable local EEG embeddings, and prototype-based attention aggregates decision-relevant temporal evidence during progressive observation.
AI.result: Offline evaluations across three EEG paradigms showed state-of-the-art accuracy-time trade-offs and strong cross-paradigm generalizability; an online human-in-the-loop AR-based BCI experiment demonstrated real-time feasibility.
AI.conclusion: ProtoTrigger offers a general EEG state encoding framework for efficient ATDM-based BCI systems.

title: Correlation-Guided Flow Matching with Annealed Masking for Spatial Transcriptomics Generation
summary: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) provides spatially resolved gene expression profiling but remains expensive, motivating the prediction of ST from histology images. Generative models have emerged as a mainstream paradigm for ST prediction due to their ability to model the conditional distribution of gene expression and capture its inherent stochasticity. However, these methods typically treat genes as independent prediction targets and overlook the intrinsic gene-gene interactions in biological systems, which limits their ability to preserve biologically meaningful co-expression patterns. We argue that gene-gene interactions, which reflect shared pathways and regulatory mechanisms, are essential for generating numerically accurate and biologically coherent ST profiles. In this paper, we propose CorrFlow, a correlation-guided flow matching framework for histology-to-ST prediction that explicitly models gene-gene dependencies through two complementary mechanisms. First, we introduce an annealed masked flow matching strategy, where subsets of genes are progressively masked following a timestep-dependent annealing schedule, encouraging the model to infer masked genes conditioned on the remaining genes and promoting joint conditional modeling beyond per-gene marginal estimation. Second, we devise a gene graph-regularized optimization scheme that integrates prior knowledge from the STRING database and data-driven co-expression estimated by WGCNA to construct a gene affinity graph, which enforces both local consistency and global smoothness in the predicted expression. Extensive experiments across 12 datasets show that CorrFlow achieves the best average PCC and HPCC among evaluated methods, leading to more biologically coherent ST predictions.

AI.tldr: CorrFlow, a correlation-guided flow matching framework, predicts spatial transcriptomics from histology images by explicitly modeling gene-gene dependencies via annealed masked flow matching and a gene graph-regularized optimization scheme, achieving superior PCC and HPCC across 12 datasets.
AI.motivation: Spatial transcriptomics is expensive, motivating prediction from histology images. Existing generative models treat genes as independent targets, ignoring gene-gene interactions that reflect shared pathways and regulatory mechanisms, thus limiting preservation of biologically meaningful co-expression patterns.
AI.method: CorrFlow uses two mechanisms: (1) annealed masked flow matching, progressively masking gene subsets per a timestep-dependent annealing schedule to promote joint conditional modeling beyond per-gene marginal estimation; (2) a gene graph-regularized optimization scheme using STRING database prior knowledge plus WGCNA-derived co-expression to build a gene affinity graph, enforcing local consistency and global smoothness.
AI.result: Across 12 datasets, CorrFlow achieves the best average PCC and HPCC among evaluated methods, yielding more biologically coherent ST predictions.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling gene-gene interactions is essential for numerically accurate and biologically coherent ST prediction, and CorrFlow demonstrates this via correlation-guided flow matching.

title: Testing Two-State Access in Brain and Language Model: Human EEG Reproduction, Simulation Audit, and a Proposed Model Assay
comment: 32 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Data and code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22741885
summary: Brains and the hardware of artificial neural networks are both organized ordinary matter, and whether an artificial system's organization can support consciousness remains open. This paper examines one proposed mechanism, access to a capacity-limited global workspace, through one prediction of the global neuronal workspace theory: near threshold, the single-trial response distribution is a mixture of two states rather than a continuum. Two completed analyses are reported. First, the published competing-model test of that prediction is reproduced from the authors' code on the open EEG data of twenty participants. In the active session the two-state model's protected exceedance probability first exceeds 0.95 at the same 315 ms window, with a modest predictive advantage of about 0.003 nat per trial and optimizer-sensitive interval edges; in the passive session, an additional analysis, a graded comparator ranks highest without an across-window decision. Second, a held-out family comparison proposed for transferring the test to language-model representations is calibrated in simulation at one layer: it made no false two-state call in 12,000 datasets under twelve graded nulls, but its concept-cluster interval under-covered in six settings, down to 0.22, so a replacement interval must be validated before any confirmatory use. The proposed model study, with a natural-text evidence dose, a target bridge and a state-conditional causal test, is specified but not run. No claim about experience is made.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether access to a capacity-limited global workspace (a proposed consciousness mechanism) holds, by reproducing a global neuronal workspace theory prediction (a two-state mixture near threshold) on open EEG data and calibrating a held-out family comparison for transferring the test to language-model representations.
AI.motivation: Whether an artificial system's organization can support consciousness is open. This paper examines one proposed mechanism—access to a capacity-limited global workspace—via a testable prediction of global neuronal workspace theory.
AI.method: Two completed analyses: (1) reproducing the published competing-model test of the two-state (vs. continuum) prediction from the authors' code on open EEG data of twenty participants (active and passive sessions); (2) calibrating in simulation (at one layer) a held-out family comparison meant to transfer the test to language-model representations, under twelve graded nulls. AI.result: Reproduction: in the active session the two-state model's protected exceedance probability first exceeds 0.95 at the same 315 ms window, with ~0.003 nat/trial predictive advantage and optimizer-sensitive interval edges; in the passive session a graded comparator ranks highest without an across-window decision. AI.conclusion: The two-state prediction is reproducible in the active session and the transfer test shows no false positives in simulation, but interval miscalibration must be fixed. The confirmatory model study is specified but not run, and no claim about experience is made.

title: Spike Sorting with VanillaSort
summary: Training spike detectors on real recordings is challenging because algorithmically generated labels can be noisy and incomplete. We propose VanillaSort, combining multichannel detection with spatially augmented, template-guided clustering. VanillaDet uses visibility-aware masking, truncated Gaussian targets and a temporally tolerant positive-bag loss, followed by conditional event-SNR gating. VanillaCluster combines HuiduRep embeddings with relative-amplitude features for Gaussian mixture clustering and refines assignments using cross-fitted waveform templates built from selected core events. VanillaDet improves detection accuracy over SimSort by two and three percentage points on the static and drift subsets of Hybrid Janelia, respectively. The complete pipeline also improves sorting performance over the corresponding HuiduRep baselines. These results support learning from imperfect real-data labels and incorporating waveform consistency into neuronal assignment.

AI.tldr: VanillaSort combines multichannel spike detection (VanillaDet) with template-guided clustering (VanillaCluster) to learn effectively from noisy, incomplete real-recording labels, improving detection and sorting over SimSort and HuiduRep baselines.
AI.motivation: Training spike detectors on real recordings is hard because algorithmically generated labels are noisy and incomplete, limiting the quality of supervised learning.
AI.method: VanillaSort has two parts. VanillaDet performs multichannel detection using visibility-aware masking, truncated Gaussian targets, a temporally tolerant positive-bag loss, and conditional event-SNR gating. VanillaCluster combines HuiduRep embeddings with relative-amplitude features in a Gaussian mixture model, then refines assignments via cross-fitted waveform templates built from selected core events.
AI.result: VanillaDet improves detection accuracy over SimSort by 2 and 3 percentage points on the static and drift subsets of Hybrid Janelia. The full pipeline also outperforms the corresponding HuiduRep sorting baselines.
AI.conclusion: Results support learning from imperfect real-data labels and incorporating waveform consistency into neuronal assignment.

title: Asymptotics and finite sample bounds for prediction and smoothing in Wright-Fisher hidden Markov models
summary: We study prediction and smoothing in hidden Markov models with a latent signal given by a multi-type Wright-Fisher diffusion and discrete-time categorical observations, motivated by repeated-sampling time-series settings, including temporally binned ancient-DNA data, in which noisy frequency counts are recorded at finitely many times. Our focus is on the exact Bayesian predictive and smoothing distributions available under parent-independent mutation, in relation to their large-sample targets under repeated within-time sampling. For a fixed collection-time grid and diverging within-time sample sizes, we show that the exact Wright-Fisher predictive and smoothing distributions converge in total variation to the corresponding population transition and bridge laws at the limiting neighboring frequencies. We then derive explicit finite-sample control for the predictive law and a corresponding finite-sample bound for the marginal smoother. Finally, at the inspection times, we show that the joint conditional law concentrates at the target frequencies and that its active coordinates are asymptotically Gaussian, while coordinates with zero true frequencies converge to Gamma limits at faster rates. Our regime imposes no restriction on dependence across inspection times beyond within-time sampling. The analysis rests on a fixed-interval tail bound for Kingman's coalescent block-counting process, which is of independent interest.

AI.tldr: Exact Bayesian prediction and smoothing in Wright-Fisher HMMs with categorical observations converge in total variation to population transition/bridge laws as within-time sample sizes diverge, with explicit finite-sample bounds and asymptotic normality/Gamma limits at inspection times.
AI.motivation: Motivated by repeated-sampling time-series settings such as temporally binned ancient-DNA data, where noisy frequency counts are observed at finitely many times. The goal is to relate exact Bayesian predictive/smoothing distributions under a Wright-Fisher latent signal to their large-sample population targets.
AI.method: Studies hidden Markov models with a multi-type Wright-Fisher diffusion latent signal and discrete-time categorical observations under parent-independent mutation. For a fixed collection-time grid with diverging within-time sample sizes, proves convergence in total variation of exact predictive and smoothing distributions to population transition and bridge laws. Derives finite-sample control via a fixed-interval tail bound for Kingman's coalescent block-counting process. Uses asymptotic analysis of the joint conditional law at inspection times.
AI.result: Exact Wright-Fisher predictive and smoothing distributions converge in total variation to population transition and bridge laws at limiting neighboring frequencies. Explicit finite-sample bounds obtained for the predictive law and the marginal smoother. At inspection times, the joint conditional law concentrates at target frequencies; active coordinates are asymptotically Gaussian, while zero-true-frequency coordinates converge to Gamma limits at faster rates.
AI.conclusion: Establishes rigorous large-sample convergence and finite-sample guarantees for Bayesian inference in Wright-Fisher HMMs without restricting dependence across inspection times beyond within-time sampling. The Kingman coalescent tail bound is of independent interest.

title: Experimental Design for Controller Selection in Synthetic Biology
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Accepted to the 65th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC 2026)
summary: Synthetic biology enables the design of genetic circuits that act as feedback controllers. These controllers are typically designed using computational models, but mismatch between model and real dynamics can lead to controllers that fail in practice. While methods to address this issue exist, synthetic biology introduces additional structural constraints. Genetic circuits are often highly constrained by experimental limitations, reducing controller design to selection among a limited set of implementable circuits rather than an optimization over a continuous space. As a result, multiple system hypotheses may lead to the same optimal controller within the implementable set. Reducing model uncertainty may therefore be irrelevant when the models lead to the same optimal controller. In this paper, we exploit this structure to develop an algorithm for controller selection in synthetic biology, formulating the problem as a decision-oriented experimental design problem over a finite controller set. We represent plant uncertainty using a set of hypotheses and select experiments to minimize the posterior controller selection risk, rather than global model uncertainty. Across three mechanistic case studies, our method reaches the stopping criterion in fewer experimental rounds than model uncertainty and random experiment selection policies, while maintaining a comparable success rate.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates controller selection in synthetic biology as a decision-oriented experimental design problem, selecting experiments to reduce posterior controller selection risk rather than global model uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Genetic feedback controllers designed via computational models often fail due to model-reality mismatch. However, synthetic biology imposes structural constraints: circuits are limited to a small set of implementable designs, so design reduces to selection among finite candidates rather than continuous optimization. Consequently, multiple model hypotheses may map to the same optimal implementable controller, making global model uncertainty reduction wasteful or irrelevant.
AI.method: The authors exploit this structure by casting controller selection as a decision-oriented experimental design problem over a finite controller set. Plant uncertainty is represented as a set of hypotheses, and experiments are chosen to minimize the posterior controller selection risk instead of global model uncertainty.
AI.result: Across three mechanistic case studies, the method reaches the stopping criterion in fewer experimental rounds than both model-uncertainty-based and random experiment selection policies, while maintaining a comparable success rate.
AI.conclusion: Focusing experimental design on decision-relevant (controller selection) uncertainty, rather than global model uncertainty, yields more efficient controller selection in synthetic biology under structural constraints.

title: Reconstructed holograms and explanation-aware evaluation for low-cost computational pollen analysis in veterinary cytology
comment: 25 pages, 17 figures, 20 tables. Supplementary material included. Submitted to a journal for peer review
summary: Automated pollen analysis supports veterinary cytology, but brightfield microscopy is costlier and more complex than lens-less digital in-line holographic microscopy. We evaluate whether reconstructed holograms can narrow this gap and whether model explanations remain reliable under modality change. Six pollen species were imaged by brightfield and holographic microscopy. Raw, single back-propagation and iterative phase retrieval holograms were evaluated with YOLOv26s detection and MobileNetV4 classification after anchor-based annotation transfer. Six attribution methods were assessed for spatial grounding and faithfulness with the Attribution Health Inspection and Repair (AHIR) protocol, which tests model brittleness under weak noise and corrects attribution-map granularity when needed. Brightfield achieved 0.6890 mAP50-95 (0.8865 mAP50) for detection and 0.9687 macro-F1 (0.9705 accuracy) for classification. Reconstructed holograms narrowed the gap with a task-dependent split: p-type was strongest for detection at 0.5324 mAP50-95 (0.8229 mAP50), while r-type was strongest for classification at 0.7695 macro-F1 (0.7866 accuracy), both far above raw-hologram baselines. Activation-based explanations localized strongly on grains, and region-based methods retained ~60 to ~80% of faithfulness under holography. The holographic detector was highly brittle to weak perturbations, saturating deletion-based evaluation while insertion remained informative. Pixel-level gradient explanations approached random floor, yet spatial smoothing restored p-type gradient faithfulness from 0.05 to 0.51. For holographic classification, perturbation-based explanations remained faithful while gradient-based methods fell below random floor. Reconstruction improves low-cost holographic pollen analysis, while AHIR distinguishes genuine attribution failure from artifacts caused by model brittleness and map granularity.

AI.tldr: Reconstructed holograms narrow the cost-gap with brightfield for pollen detection/classification, and the AHIR protocol clarifies when model explanations stay faithful under modality change.
AI.motivation: Automated pollen analysis aids veterinary cytology, but brightfield microscopy is costlier and more complex than lens-less digital in-line holographic microscopy. The study asks whether reconstructed holograms can close this gap and whether model explanations remain reliable under modality change.
AI.method: Six pollen species imaged by brightfield and holographic microscopy. Raw, single back-propagation, and iterative phase retrieval holograms evaluated with YOLOv26s detection and MobileNetV4 classification via anchor-based annotation transfer. Six attribution methods assessed for spatial grounding and faithfulness using the AHIR protocol, which tests brittleness under weak noise and corrects attribution-map granularity.

Reconstructed holograms narrowed gap task-dependently: p-type best for detection (0.5324 mAP50-95; 0.8229 mAP50), r-type best for classification (0.7695 macro-F1; 0.7866 acc), both above raw baselines. Activation-based explanations localized on grains; region-based methods retained ~60-80% faithfulness. Holographic detector brittle to weak perturbations (deletion saturated; insertion informative). Pixel-level gradients near random floor; smoothing restored p-type gradient faithfulness 0.05→0.51. For holographic classification, perturbation-based explanations stayed faithful while gradients fell below random floor.
