title: THz Spectroscopy of Urine Vapors from Patients with Prostate Cancer and Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: A Pilot Analysis
summary: Approximately 13% of men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer (PC) during their lifetime. Serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is widely used for screening and risk assessment; however, PSA elevations are not cancer-specific and may also occur in benign conditions such as prostatitis and benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Additional non-invasive approaches capable of provid- ing complementary molecular information are therefore needed. Here, we present an exploratory pilot study using high-resolution terahertz (THz) spectroscopy to examine urine-derived volatile and thermal-decomposition products. Analysis of urine samples from 24 patients with PC and 14 patients with BPH identified differences in the reported molecular-assignment patterns and candi- date spectral features for further evaluation. The study was designed for candidate identification and feasibility assessment and did not evaluate diagnostic accuracy or superiority to PSA. These findings support further investigation of THz spectroscopy as a potential source of complementary molecular information alongside PSA and other established clinical assessments. The study also outlines the technical standardization and clinical-validation requirements that must be addressed before this approach can be considered for routine clinical use.

AI.tldr: A pilot study uses high-resolution terahertz spectroscopy on urine-derived volatile and thermal-decomposition products to distinguish prostate cancer from BPH, identifying candidate spectral features but not evaluating diagnostic accuracy.
AI.motivation: Serum PSA is widely used for prostate cancer screening, but PSA elevations are not cancer-specific and can occur in benign conditions like prostatitis and BPH. There is a need for additional non-invasive approaches that provide complementary molecular information.
AI.method: Exploratory pilot study using high-resolution terahertz (THz) spectroscopy to analyze urine-derived volatile and thermal-decomposition products from 24 prostate cancer patients and 14 BPH patients, examining molecular-assignment patterns and candidate spectral features.
AI.result: Differences were identified in reported molecular-assignment patterns and candidate spectral features between PC and BPH groups. The study did not evaluate diagnostic accuracy or superiority to PSA.
AI.conclusion: Findings support further investigation of THz spectroscopy as a complementary molecular information source alongside PSA. Technical standardization and clinical-validation requirements must be addressed before routine clinical use.

title: A discrete generative model of neuronal spiking activity on microelectrode arrays
summary: Generative models of neural activity could help characterize tissue dynamics, compare experimental conditions, and simulate population activity for applications ranging from disease and drug-response studies to closed-loop experimentation. Existing approaches, however, typically assume a fixed set of sorted neurons, whereas high-density microelectrode arrays produce extremely sparse, array-wide binary spike volumes in which the observed subset of electrodes varies across assays. We introduce a discrete generative model that represents this activity using a shared vocabulary of spatiotemporal motifs. A residual vector-quantized autoencoder learns the motif vocabulary, while a factorized masked transformer predicts where activity occurs and which motif appears at each active location. We evaluate the model on 31 assays spanning human brain organoids and acute \emph{ex vivo} human hippocampal tissue. The learned motifs are broadly reused: assay identity explains only $9%$ of the entropy in motif use, and motif overlap across tissue types is comparable to overlap within them. When representation quality is evaluated independently of the generative prior, our approach achieves $5.2\times$ the voxel-level reconstruction average precision of a matched flat tokenizer. For masked completion and free generation, the full model achieves $1.4$--$2.6\times$ the site-level average precision of the matched generative baseline and outperforms it across all four families of generation metrics. These results establish a compact, reusable representation for array-wide spiking activity without learned assay-specific parameters, providing a scalable foundation for generative modeling across diverse neural preparations.

AI.tldr: A discrete generative model using a shared vocabulary of spatiotemporal motifs models array-wide binary spiking activity, achieving better reconstruction and generation than baselines across 31 human brain organoid and hippocampal tissue assays.
AI.motivation: Existing generative models of neural activity assume a fixed set of sorted neurons, but high-density microelectrode arrays produce sparse, array-wide binary spike volumes where the observed electrode subset varies across assays, limiting generalization.
AI.method: A residual vector-quantized autoencoder learns a shared vocabulary of spatiotemporal motifs, while a factorized masked transformer predicts where activity occurs and which motif appears at each active location.
AI.result: Evaluated on 31 assays (human brain organoids and ex vivo hippocampal tissue): motifs are broadly reused (assay identity explains only 9% of motif-use entropy; cross-tissue overlap comparable to within-tissue). Reconstruction achieves 5.2x voxel-level average precision over a matched flat tokenizer; masked completion and free generation achieve 1.4-2.6x site-level average precision, outperforming baseline across all four generation metric families.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a compact, reusable representation for array-wide spiking activity without assay-specific parameters, offering a scalable foundation for generative modeling across diverse neural preparations.

title: Matched-Input Estimates Differ in Sign Across Architectures: Auditing EEG Foundation Models on Motor Imagery
summary: Pretrained EEG foundation models are increasingly proposed as general-purpose encoders for brain-computer interfaces, yet recent benchmarks disagree about when their representations transfer to downstream tasks. We audit LaBraM and CBraMod on motor imagery under a validation-locked protocol in which preprocessing, architecture, optimization, freeze depth, checkpoint, temperature, and method selection are determined using training-session data only. On four-class BCI Competition IV-2a, every supervised comparator evaluated here outperforms every foundation-model configuration, including validation-selected fine-tuning. We then examine a key confound: foundation models and task-specific decoders are normally evaluated using different input pipelines. Retraining three supervised architectures on the broadband arrays consumed by the foundation models produces matched-input accuracy differences of opposite sign across architectures: broadband input improves ATCNet by 0.078 accuracy while reducing EEG Conformer accuracy by 0.088. None of the three individual matched-input terms is significant after multiple-comparison correction at n = 9, so we treat the sign variation descriptively rather than as a formal architecture-by-pipeline interaction. These observed sign differences suggest that a single comparator may not provide an architecture-invariant decomposition of a pretrained-versus-supervised performance gap. The four-class deficit also does not reproduce uniformly across motor-imagery datasets: on two-class BNCI2014-004 we cannot detect the same separation between fine-tuned CBraMod and the supervised comparators. Finally, validation-fitted temperature scaling returns foundation-model calibration error to the supervised range despite substantially lower four-class accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper audits EEG foundation models (LaBraM, CBraMod) on motor imagery under a validation-locked protocol. Supervised baselines beat all foundation-model configs on 4-class BCI IV-2a; the gap is confounded by mismatched input pipelines and does not reproduce on 2-class BNCI2014-004.
AI.motivation: Pretrained EEG foundation models are proposed as general-purpose BCI encoders, but existing benchmarks disagree on whether their representations transfer. The authors suspect evaluation confounds—especially differing input pipelines between foundation models and task-specific decoders—may explain the disagreement.
AI.method: A validation-locked audit of LaBraM and CBraMod on motor imagery: preprocessing, architecture, optimization, freeze depth, checkpoint, temperature, and method selection are fixed using training-session data only. Supervised comparators (ATCNet, EEG Conformer, etc.) are also retrained on the broadband input arrays consumed by the foundation models to create matched-input comparisons (n=9).
AI.result: On 4-class BCI IV-2a, every supervised comparator outperforms every foundation-model configuration. Matched-input retraining yields sign-varying differences across architectures (ATCNet +0.078, EEG Conformer -0.088), none individually significant after correction at n=9. The 4-class deficit does not reproduce on 2-class BNCI2014-004. Validation-fitted temperature scaling brings foundation-model calibration error into the supervised range despite lower accuracy.
AI.conclusion: A single comparator may not give an architecture-invariant decomposition of the pretrained-versus-supervised gap, and reported deficits are dataset-dependent. Evaluation protocols must control for input-pipeline confounds and avoid assuming uniform transfer advantages.

title: Vision Transformers versus convolutional neural networks for fine-grained orchid genus identification in a species-rich, data-poor flora: a controlled benchmark on the Orchidaceae of New Guinea
summary: New Guinea is the world's richest island flora (~2,856 orchid species), yet most species are represented by only a handful of photographs, far fewer than direct species-level classification requires. Methods for fine-grained identification in such species-rich, data-poor floras are needed, and it remains unclear which backbone architecture and pretraining strategy best support them. We built a two-stage system that first predicts the genus of a query photograph, then retrieves visually similar reference images of candidate species using FAISS. We compared four pretrained backbones -- two Vision Transformers (ViTs; DINOv2, BioCLIP 2) and two CNNs (ConvNeXt V2-L, EfficientNetV2-L) -- fine-tuned under an identical protocol on a fixed, species-stratified partition of 16,701 photographs spanning 120 genera and 1,350 species, assessing accuracy, calibration, error structure, species retrieval, and open-set detection of novel genera. DINOv2 attained the best genus performance (macro top-1 66.9%, 95% CI 63.7-70.6; global top-1 88.9%); both ViTs outranked both CNNs, and general-purpose self-supervised pretraining (DINOv2) outperformed domain-matched biological pretraining (BioCLIP 2) by 7.1 points of macro top-1. Errors concentrated on two abundant genera acting as error attractors. DINOv2 embeddings achieved species Recall@5 of 86.6% and genus Recall@5 of 98.7%; temperature scaling reduced every backbone's Expected Calibration Error to about 0.03; and a distance-based open-set gate flagged unseen genera (mean AUROC 0.958). A self-supervised Vision-Transformer backbone combined with embedding retrieval is an effective, deployable strategy for fine-grained identification in species-rich, data-poor floras. The system is released as an open web application (the New Guinea Orchid Identifier), offering a practical template for other hyperdiverse, under-documented taxa.

AI.tldr: A two-stage orchid identification system for New Guinea uses a self-supervised ViT (DINOv2) for genus prediction followed by FAISS-based image retrieval for species, outperforming CNNs and domain-matched pretraining while supporting open-set detection.
AI.motivation: New Guinea hosts the world's richest island flora (~2,856 orchid species), but most species have very few photographs, making direct species-level classification infeasible; it is unclear which backbone architecture and pretraining strategy best support fine-grained identification in such species-rich, data-poor floras.
AI.method: A two-stage system predicting genus from a query photo, then retrieving visually similar reference images of candidate species via FAISS. Four pretrained backbones (ViTs: DINOv2, BioCLIP 2; CNNs: ConvNeXt V2-L, EfficientNetV2-L) were fine-tuned identically on a fixed species-stratified partition of 16,701 photographs across 120 genera and 1,350 species, evaluated on accuracy, calibration, error structure, species retrieval, and open-set detection of novel genera.
AI.result: DINOv2 achieved the best genus performance (macro top-1 66.9%, 95% CI 63.7-70.6; global top-1 88.9%). Both ViTs beat both CNNs, and self-supervised pretraining (DINOv2) exceeded domain-matched biological pretraining (BioCLIP 2) by 7.1 macro top-1 points. Errors concentrated on two abundant error-attractor genera. Species Recall@5 reached 86.6% and genus Recall@5 98.7%. Temperature scaling reduced ECE to ~0.03, and a distance-based open-set gate flagged unseen genera (mean AUROC 0.958).
AI.conclusion: A self-supervised Vision-Transformer backbone with embedding retrieval is an effective, deployable strategy for fine-grained identification in species-rich, data-poor floras. Released as an open web application (New Guinea Orchid Identifier), it offers a practical template for other hyperdiverse, under-documented taxa.

title: QLoRA Fine-Tuning of Ministral LLM for Sequence-to-Function Protein Annotation
summary: Functional annotation of newly sequenced proteins remains a bottleneck in molecular biology: the number of sequences in public repositories grows far faster than the capacity for manual curation. Most computational approaches consider annotation as multi-label classification over a fixed ontology, which constrains predictions to a predefined label set. In this work we study the the protein annotation as a sequence-to-text generation problem. We fine-tune the 3B-parameter Ministral 3 base model with QLoRA (4-bit NF4 quantization with low-rank adapters) on sequence annotation pairs. We assess predictions with an LLM-as-expert protocol: a GPT model prompted as a senior molecular-biology curator scores organism identification as binary and function annotation quality. We conclude that QLoRA-fine-tuned compact LLMs can generate curator-style annotations with genuine biological value for a substantial subset of proteins. We also discuss future directions in data quality, model scaling, and evidence grounding that are needed to make the approach sufficiently reliable for practical use.

AI.tldr: This paper frames protein functional annotation as a sequence-to-text generation task, fine-tuning a 3B-parameter Ministral 3 model with QLoRA on sequence-annotation pairs and evaluating outputs via an LLM-as-expert protocol.
AI.motivation: Public sequence repositories grow far faster than manual curation capacity, making functional annotation a bottleneck. Most computational methods treat annotation as multi-label classification over a fixed ontology, restricting predictions to a predefined label set.
AI.method: The authors reframe annotation as sequence-to-text generation and fine-tune the 3B-parameter Ministral 3 base model using QLoRA (4-bit NF4 quantization with low-rank adapters) on sequence annotation pairs. Predictions are scored by an LLM-as-expert protocol in which a GPT model is prompted as a senior molecular-biology curator, providing a binary organism-identification score and a function annotation quality score.
AI.result: The QLoRA-fine-tuned compact LLM can generate curator-style annotations with genuine biological value for a substantial subset of proteins, as judged by the LLM-as-expert evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuned compact LLMs show promise for open-ended protein annotation, but reliability for practical use requires future work on data quality, model scaling, and evidence grounding.

title: A Proof of the Global Attractor Conjecture in a Special Case
comment: 17 pages, no figures and tables. AI assisted, acknowledgement declaration included
summary: We prove the Global Attractor Conjecture for complex balanced mass-action reaction networks whose reachable siphons satisfy two structural conditions, allowing multiple linkage classes. The proof proceeds in two steps. A structural condition relating the stoichiometric space to the reactions active within a boundary face ensures that a stoichiometric compatibility class contains at most one boundary equilibrium with any prescribed zero set. Finiteness of the possible zero sets and connectedness of the $ω$-limit set then imply that any boundary limit set consists of a single equilibrium. To exclude convergence to such an equilibrium, we consider the embedded reaction network obtained by projecting onto the vanishing species and freezing the concentrations of the surviving species at a positive limit. The structural condition guarantees complex balance of this embedded network, while a further condition on its minimal active linkage classes ensures that an explicit Chetaev function is strictly increasing near the boundary. This excludes the boundary point as an accumulation point whenever the surviving concentrations converge. Consequently, every positive trajectory converges to the unique positive equilibrium in its stoichiometric compatibility class. Examples illustrate the hypotheses and their relation to strong endotacticity.

AI.tldr: The paper proves the Global Attractor Conjecture for complex balanced mass-action reaction networks with multiple linkage classes, under two structural conditions on reachable siphons.
AI.motivation: The Global Attractor Conjecture is a central open problem in chemical reaction network theory. Prior results often assumed a single linkage class or restrictive conditions, leaving complex balanced networks with multiple linkage classes unresolved.
AI.method: The proof has two steps: (1) a structural condition linking the stoichiometric space to reactions active on a boundary face ensures at most one boundary equilibrium per zero set; finiteness of zero sets and connectedness of the ω-limit set force any boundary limit set to be a single equilibrium. (2) An embedded network is formed by projecting onto vanishing species and freezing surviving species at a positive limit; complex balance is preserved, and a further condition on minimal active linkage classes yields an explicit strictly increasing Chetaev function near the boundary, excluding boundary accumulation.
AI.result: Boundary convergence is excluded, so every positive trajectory converges to the unique positive equilibrium in its stoichiometric compatibility class. Examples illustrate the hypotheses and their relation to strong endotacticity.
AI.conclusion: The Global Attractor Conjecture holds for complex balanced mass-action networks with reachable siphons satisfying the two stated structural conditions, allowing multiple linkage classes.

title: Experimental evidence of generalization in quantum machine learning in small-data regime
summary: Quantum machine learning is a promising paradigm for learning from limited data, a central bottleneck in domains such as medical imaging, clinical trials, and rare diseases. Quantum convolutional neural networks (QCNNs) are particularly attractive in this setting, combining a hierarchical architecture with strong inductive bias and a parameter count that grows only logarithmically with system size. Their appeal rests on the generalization bounds of Caro et al. (2022), which show that the generalization error of a quantum model scales with the number of trainable parameters rather than with the Hilbert-space dimension, placing QCNNs in a potentially sample-efficient regime. We develop a hardware-compatible QCNN with mid-circuit measurement and classical feed-forward, and show on a binary handwritten-digit task that strong test performance is achievable from as few as 10 training samples, with the generalization error decreasing as the training set grows. At a matched 45-parameter budget the QCNN learns where an equally small classical convolutional network stays at chance, although an unconstrained classical baseline with roughly 25,000 parameters remains strongest when data are plentiful. Transpiling amplitude and angle encoded circuits across image resolutions from 2x2 to 512x512 pixels then exposes the dominant scaling bottleneck: amplitude encoding stays qubit-efficient but grows extremely deep, whereas angle encoding stays shallow but becomes qubit-prohibitive. On the medically motivated BreastMNIST benchmark the QCNN does not surpass the unconstrained classical network, yet it learns consistently above chance using orders of magnitude fewer parameters. Our results indicate that for QCNNs, learning from few samples is attainable in practice, whereas scaling to realistic image data is constrained less by optimization than by data encoding and hardware execution.

AI.tldr: A hardware-compatible QCNN with mid-circuit measurement and feed-forward learns binary digit classification from as few as 10 samples, with generalization error scaling with parameter count, but data encoding and hardware execution dominate scaling limits rather than optimization.
AI.motivation: Quantum machine learning promises learning from limited data, a key bottleneck in medical imaging, clinical trials, and rare diseases. QCNNs are attractive due to hierarchical architecture, strong inductive bias, and logarithmically growing parameter count. Caro et al. (2022) generalization bounds suggest QCNNs may be sample-efficient since generalization error scales with trainable parameters rather than Hilbert-space dimension.
AI.method: Developed a hardware-compatible QCNN with mid-circuit measurement and classical feed-forward. Tested on a binary handwritten-digit task with varying training set sizes and a matched 45-parameter budget against a classical CNN. Then transpiled amplitude and angle encoded circuits across image resolutions from 2x2 to 512x512 pixels. Also evaluated on the BreastMNIST benchmark.
AI.result: Strong test performance from as few as 10 training samples, with generalization error decreasing as training set grows. At matched 45 parameters, QCNN learns while the small classical CNN stays at chance, though an unconstrained classical baseline (~25,000 parameters) is strongest with plentiful data. Amplitude encoding is qubit-efficient but extremely deep; angle encoding is shallow but qubit-prohibitive. On BreastMNIST, QCNN does not surpass the unconstrained classical network but learns consistently above chance with orders of magnitude fewer parameters.
AI.conclusion: For QCNNs, learning from few samples is attainable in practice. Scaling to realistic image data is constrained less by optimization than by data encoding and hardware execution.

title: Towards Accurate Prediction of Mutation-Induced Changes in Protein Structure
summary: Proteins can possess numerous mutations relative to their wild-type amino acid sequences with minimal impact to their structure and function. However, in other cases, even a single amino acid mutation relative to the wild-type sequence can lead to a large change in structure or even a disease phenotype. While the accuracy of wild-type protein structure prediction has improved significantly in recent years, it remains difficult to accurately predict the structure of mutant proteins. Here, we characterize the local mutation-induced structural changes in proteins for a dataset of wildtype and the corresponding single-amino acid mutant x-ray crystal structures from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). We find that mutation-induced structural changes in these proteins are localized at the site of the mutation, decaying rapidly with increasing spatial distance from the mutation site. In addition, we evaluate how well AlphaFold3 can recapitulate the observed mutation-induced structural deformations in the x-ray crystal structures. We find that the accuracy of the AlphaFold3 predictions decreases strongly with increasing mutation-induced deformation. In contrast to the results for AlphaFold3, the Pearson correlation between a single physical feature, i.e. the change in solvent accessibility, and the mutation-induced deformation does not depend on the magnitude of the deformation. Our results and analyses provide a framework for further studies aimed at predicting the structural changes in proteins caused by single amino acid mutations.

AI.tldr: This study characterizes local mutation-induced structural changes in single-amino-acid mutant crystal structures from the PDB and shows that AlphaFold3's accuracy degrades strongly as mutation-induced deformation increases, whereas a simple solvent-accessibility feature correlates independently of deformation magnitude.
AI.motivation: While wild-type protein structure prediction has improved markedly, predicting mutant protein structures remains difficult. Even a single amino acid mutation can leave structure and function largely intact or cause large structural changes and disease, so understanding the nature and predictability of mutation-induced structural changes is important.
AI.method: The authors assembled a dataset of wild-type and corresponding single-amino-acid mutant x-ray crystal structures from the Protein Data Bank and characterized local mutation-induced structural changes, analyzing how these changes decay with spatial distance from the mutation site. They then evaluated AlphaFold3's ability to recapitulate the observed deformations and compared it with a single physical feature: change in solvent accessibility.
AI.result: Mutation-induced structural changes are localized at the mutation site and decay rapidly with increasing spatial distance. AlphaFold3 prediction accuracy decreases strongly as mutation-induced deformation grows. In contrast, the Pearson correlation between change in solvent accessibility and mutation-induced deformation is independent of deformation magnitude.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide a framework for future work aimed at predicting the structural changes in proteins caused by single amino acid mutations, highlighting limitations of AlphaFold3 for large-deformation mutants and the potential utility of simple physical features like solvent accessibility.

title: Nucleosome simulations suggest mechanisms of electrostatically-driven mesoscale chromatin evolution
summary: Nucleosomes are structures made up of proteins called histones that bind and compact DNA, driving the mesoscale organization of the chromatin polymer. Although histone proteins have diversified over evolutionary time, their contributions to the corresponding diversification of chromatin structure are poorly understood. Here, we mine protein databases for histones and create \emph{in silico} nucleosomes for 3241 organisms spanning $>$1.5B years of evolution. Using a combination of electrostatic calculations and coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations, we reveal extensive biophysical diversification of the nucleosome unit. Finally, we perform coarse-grained oligonucleosomal simulations on a subset of evolutionarily and biophysically divergent nucleosomes, demonstrating dramatic differences in bulk phase behavior of chromatin. Taken together, our results suggest a paradigm in which histones may have evolved to facilitate particular types of mesoscale chromatin behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper mines histone sequences across 3241 organisms spanning >1.5B years of evolution, builds in silico nucleosomes, and uses electrostatics plus coarse-grained simulations to show extensive biophysical diversification of nucleosomes that leads to dramatically different chromatin phase behavior.
AI.motivation: Histone proteins have diversified over evolutionary time, but how this diversification translates into corresponding changes in chromatin structure is poorly understood.
AI.method: Mining protein databases for histones, constructing in silico nucleosomes for 3241 organisms (>1.5B years of evolution), combining electrostatic calculations with coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations, and performing coarse-grained oligonucleosomal simulations on a subset of evolutionarily and biophysically divergent nucleosomes.
AI.result: Extensive biophysical diversification of the nucleosome unit was revealed, and oligonucleosomal simulations demonstrated dramatic differences in bulk phase behavior of chromatin.
AI.conclusion: Histones may have evolved to facilitate particular types of mesoscale chromatin behavior, suggesting a paradigm linking histone evolution to chromatin mesoscale organization.
